prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in lyric poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture of exceptional imaginative and formal ambition

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged. The citation is narrower than in round 1. B043 still best satisfies the common criteria together: an unmistakable voice, formal ambition matched by formal control, and a project that accumulates across poetry and prose, not a single peak. The round-1 exchange tested this and did not overturn it. All six files share the same reservations I hold: translation dependence, digression versus depth, and thin poetry coverage. Those reservations apply to the evidence the committee has, not to a rival candidate. I also compared the alternatives on the criterion the chair asked about, namely which gives the firmest basis for a whole-oeuvre judgment. Adonis has a very large poetic project and a durable influence on Arabic poetic language, but the achievement lies in prosody and diction that I can judge only at second hand. Olsson's doubt about the late work is a specific point I cannot resolve. Carson has very high voice and formal invention. Her original achievement seems to rest on a few landmark books, and Olsson, Palm and Sem-Sandberg have all named the translations, adaptations and book-object work as a difficulty for a whole-oeuvre citation. B043 is the case in which the load-bearing evidence consists of original works across decades. I do not count the unanimity of round 1 as merit. The preference rests on the arguments above. What changed is the wording. I drop 'lifetime's work', claims of completeness or encyclopedic mastery, and any assertion of lineage that I cannot argue from the texts. I keep poetry as the lyric root of the prose, not as a co-equal pillar, because translated coverage of the poetry is thinner. On the chair's question about what would lower B043: I would lower it if readers of the later novels, especially in Romanian, reported that they repeat the earlier project rather than extend it, or if the long books proved uneven in a way the best-known ones conceal.
statement.case_against: The main weakness remains evidential. His effect lies in sentence rhythm, syntactic density and digression, and I know it through translation and critical report, not in the Romanian. Maximalism is not depth in itself, and the committee has not established which volumes beyond Blinding and Solenoid show sustained quality. Public knowledge points to other works, such as Nostalgia, Levantul and the later prose, that would test this, but I have not verified how they read or how they translate. The inward mode may also limit breadth of significance, as Sward argues, and I can answer that only partly. If the committee concludes that the digression is excess across much of the corpus, or that the poetry cannot be read well enough to support the 'rooted in lyric poetry' clause, the case weakens. Adonis or Carson would then deserve a closer second look. That would not make either of them a safe alternative, given the translation limits already recorded for Adonis and the question of original oeuvre for Carson.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu from second to first and kept Carson as his first alternative. He reads her translations and scholarship as part of one sustained engagement with antiquity that feeds her original work, not only as a complication. He also doubts that Adonis's late poetry is as distinguished as the early and middle work.
responses.response: I accept Olsson's correction that the engagement with antiquity may be one continuing project, not scattered side work, and I withdraw any suggestion that it is merely a complication. It still leaves the question I care about under 'whole oeuvre': what the citation could say about original achievement without leaning on a few books and on the printed object, which cannot be assessed from text alone. That is why Carson stays my second alternative and not my lead. Olsson's point about Adonis's late work is the most specific substantive doubt on the table. It affects how safe the alternative is, since a poet who is strongest early and in the middle is a different case from one who is sustained throughout. I cannot test it in Arabic. I would ask whether any member or expert can speak to it, and I would not treat the doubt as settled either way.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranked Adonis sixth only because he cannot test the language-level claim, and he asked for Arabic readers or reliable critical testimony. He shares the gap in poetry coverage for Cărtărescu and says it limits how much weight the poetry can carry in the citation, but is not a reason to drop it.
responses.response: I agree that the limit on weight is the right way to put it, and I have made that change. Poetry is named as the root of the prose, not as an equal claim. His answer on Adonis is honest, but the same standard has to hold for both. If a member cannot test Arabic prosody and so discounts Adonis, the same member cannot test Romanian prose rhythm either. Either both rest on translation and critical report with the uncertainty recorded, or both need expert testimony. I do not say this to argue for Adonis. I say it so that translation dependence does not decide the matter selectively. It is also why I keep B021 as an alternative while preferring B043. My preference rests on the greater amount of original work that a committee can read in translation, not on the absence of a language barrier.

responses.point: Palm separates sustained ambition from sustained quality. She says the density question should be kept open and not settled by enthusiasm, and that the citation should give the prose the weight and mention the poetry only as part of the oeuvre. She ranks Adonis lower because she cannot assess the Arabic.
responses.response: Her distinction is the one I use. Ambition is visible in the descriptions of the books. Quality across the whole corpus is what we have not shown. My answer is therefore conditional. The case holds if the later books extend the project, and I have listed what would change my view. I follow her on citation wording and have taken out claims that go beyond the evidence. On the translation question I put in round 1, her round-1 reply says she rates Adonis lower because she cannot assess the language-level achievement, and I read that as a statement about her own access, not about the poetry. I accept that. If original-language testimony for either Arabic or Romanian is available to the committee, it should count for more than any of our translated readings.

responses.point: Sward asks whether the inward, maximalist mode limits breadth of significance. She says the citation should rest mainly on the large prose works and mention poetry only as a root. She ranks Adonis first among her alternatives and Carson last.
responses.response: The breadth objection is the strongest criticism of B043 and I cannot dismiss it. What I can offer is evidence of range within the mode: bodily, autobiographical, comic, grotesque and speculative material, and a movement between verse and prose. I cannot demonstrate from public knowledge that this amounts to significance as broad as the scale suggests. I would not call it solipsistic, but I would accept that the question is a real disagreement. I agree with her on the citation. On Carson I differ in one respect. I do not treat the will's wording as an obstacle for hybrid work as such, and I think the question is how much original work is central. I would not want a ranking to turn on category alone.

responses.point: Mattson says a fair assessment must rest on the full oeuvre, not only the best-known long books. She would build the citation on the prose and mention poetry only if the committee can read enough of it. She keeps Michon as an alternative for his concentration.
responses.response: I take that as a test of my own position. I cannot fully meet it, since my knowledge of the poetry and essays is thinner than of the novels, and I have recorded that. It is why the citation says 'rooted in lyric poetry' and not 'prose and poetry'. On Michon, I accept that concentration is a real achievement and that her argument for it is formal. We differ only on the weight of a small corpus under the whole-oeuvre criterion, and I do not place Michon among my two alternatives. If the committee preferred depth in a few books to range across many, the comparison should be argued on that criterion and not on how members were ranked.

uncertainties: Sentence-level achievement in Romanian, and in Arabic for Adonis, can be assessed only through translations and critical reports. I have not independently verified any source or reread any text.
Which works beyond Blinding and Solenoid best show whether the quality is sustained is not established. I cannot say from reading whether the later novels extend or repeat the earlier project.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and essays in translation is thinner than for the novels, so the clause 'rooted in lyric poetry' rests on partial evidence.
Whether the inward, maximalist mode supports significance across the whole body of work, or only within its own mode, is a live disagreement that the evidence does not resolve.

Whether Adonis's late work sustains the level of his early and middle poetry is raised by Olsson and cannot be tested by me in Arabic. How much of Carson's original work, once translations and adaptations are set aside, can carry a whole-oeuvre citation is also unsettled.
Carlberg's actual committee voting status is undocumented, so this simulated vote is a modeling assumption and not a claim about real proceedings.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, professional or family connection to any shortlisted writer. My role as Permanent Secretary and my own non-fiction practice are institutional and literary context, not evidence of a preference. My actual committee voting status is undocumented, so the simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
